doc.title: Frank Alkyer interviewed by Monk Rowe, New Orleans, Louisiana, January 10, 2020

chapter: Writing about jazz and reviewing records
title: Editorial oversight: a nasty Gap Mangione review and the Sandoval apology
summary: Rowe recalls a harsh late-1970s review of Gap Mangione. Alkyer says he acts as ombudsman and tells of apologizing to Arturo Sandoval for unbalanced reviews.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Record labels, producers and the business of making albums

blocks.x: I don’t know why, you just said something that reminded me, this was before your tenure, I think it was the late 70s. I remember a review by a release by Gap Mangione. And I sort of knew Gap, not at the time, but I knew Chuck. But it was Gap’s record. And apparently on the liner notes the writer was celebrating the chemistry of the trio. So the reviewer wrote: “If this is chemistry then women are wearing concrete underwear.” And I was like, “Did I just read that?” And I’m not sure I got the exact — but that was the thrust of it. And he was really, really nasty on this review. And boy, I guess I pictured Gap reading that. So my follow up question is do you or does someone have like veto power, like if somebody writes that kind of thing that’s so —

There are times where an editor will say, or I’ll say if it comes up to me, I end up being the ombudsman for the company. You know people can’t decide what to do with things or there’s an argument whether we should do this or do that, the editors will come to me with that kind of problem and then we’ll work out a solution. But yeah, if we think the writer is being unfair, and there are times where it slips through because it doesn’t seem that way to us, and then later on I’ll go yeah, right, if the artist comes — you know sometimes the artist will call. Sometimes the artist will complain. And if they’re correct

then I’ll say yeah you’re absolutely right. Arturo Sandoval one time, we did a double review of two records of his. One got two stars, one got four stars. And I went to see Arturo live. And he goes, “Frank, what are you doing?” I go, “What’s the problem?” He goes, “Those reviews were awful.” I go, “Arturo what are you talking about?” He goes, “The four star review, all you talked about were the negatives in the review. In the two star review you only talked about the song that he liked.” And I go, “Really?” And I went back and I read it and I wrote him an apology letter. I said, “You are absolutely a hundred percent right.” And I sat down with the editorial staff and I go, “This is an example of how we can go wrong. Just look at this. We’re journalists. We have to like figure out — we always have to like say what are we doing wrong. What’s wrong with this piece that we’re writing, and try to, you know, it’s kind of a weird way to live, but we’re always looking for what’s wrong and correct the spelling, correct this, correct the grammar, correct the thought process. Every word was spelled right. The sentences were complete. They were compelling. But the thought process was wrong. Why not tell you what you like about a good album, and why one misses maybe. And that’s all he was complaining about, and he was a hundred percent right.
Oh. A learning process all the time.
